title: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No
summary: "Access is denied" (error 5) is Windows checking rights. Every process carries a **token** saying who it runs as; every securable object has a **security descriptor** saying who may do what; and every handle is opened for specific **access rights**. This lesson explains the check, **integrity levels** and UAC, **protected processes**, and the principle of asking for no more than you need.
markdown:
## The check behind every handle When a program opens an object (a file, a process, a registry key, an event), it asks for specific rights, and Windows decides there and then: ```mermaid flowchart LR T["Your process's token
user, groups, privileges,
integrity level"] --> C{"Access check"} D["The object's security descriptor
owner, list of who may do what"] --> C R["Rights you asked for
e.g. GENERIC_READ"] --> C C -->|"allowed"| H["A handle with exactly those rights"] C -->|"denied"| E["ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (5)"] ``` - The **token** is attached to every process when it starts, inherited from the user who logged in. It lists the user, their groups (Administrators, Users...), their privileges, and an integrity level. - The **security descriptor** of an object holds an access control list (ACL): entries such as "Users: read", "Administrators: full control". - The **access mask** is the set of rights requested, as bits: for a file `FILE_READ_DATA`, `FILE_WRITE_DATA`, `DELETE`...; for a process `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION`, `PROCESS_TERMINATE`, `PROCESS_VM_READ`... The check happens **once, when the handle is opened**. The handle then carries the granted rights, and every later use is checked against them only: a file handle opened for reading cannot be used to write, whatever the user's rights. ## Ask for what you need The most common cause of error 5 in a program's own code is asking for more than it needs: `GENERIC_ALL`, `PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS`, `KEY_ALL_ACCESS`. A normal user may be allowed to read a file but not change it, and a request for all access then fails, though a request for read access would have succeeded. The fix is also the security principle of **least privilege**: request exactly the rights the code uses. ```cpp // Fails for files the user may only read: HANDLE f{ CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ | GENERIC_WRITE, ...) }; // Succeeds, and documents what the code does: HANDLE f{ CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, ...) }; ``` ## Integrity levels and UAC Each token and each object also has an **integrity level**: Low, Medium, High or System. A process cannot write to objects at a higher integrity level than its own, whatever the ACL says. | Level | Typical processes | |---|---| | Low | Sandboxed browser tabs | | Medium | Everything a user normally runs, including games | | High | Programs run "as administrator" | | System | Windows services | With **User Account Control** (UAC), even an administrator's programs normally run at Medium, with the administrator group switched off in their token. "Run as administrator" (and the consent prompt) starts a process with the **elevated** High-integrity token. This is why a game should never need elevation: it runs at Medium, writes to the user's folders (lesson 5.04), and can be compromised without giving the attacker the whole machine. ## Protected processes Some processes are **protected** (Protected Process Light, PPL): Windows' own security components, antivirus engines, and some anti-cheat services. Even an administrator cannot open them for anything beyond limited query rights, cannot read their memory, inject code into them or debug them; only code signed with specific certificates may run inside them. This is a deliberate wall: it keeps malware from tampering with security software, and it is enforced by the kernel itself. The practical lesson for tool builders: when Windows refuses access to something, that is usually the system working as designed. The tools in this course work on processes you start yourself, at the same integrity level, where the rights are yours. ## Privileges Separate from object rights, a token holds **privileges**: system-wide abilities such as `SeShutdownPrivilege` (shut down the machine), `SeLoadDriverPrivilege` (load kernel drivers) and `SeDebugPrivilege` (open any non-protected process regardless of its security descriptor). Administrators' elevated tokens contain several privileges, disabled until a program explicitly enables them with `AdjustTokenPrivileges`. Normal programs never need them; development tools like debuggers do, which is why Visual Studio asks to restart elevated when you try to attach to a process running as administrator. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Asking for all access > Request the specific rights the code uses. It succeeds more often and limits damage if the program is compromised. > [!warning] "It works as administrator, so let's always run elevated" > Find which right is missing instead. Games and tools should run as a normal user. > [!warning] Assuming error 5 means a bug in the parameters > It is a security decision. Check which rights you requested, the object's ACL, and the integrity levels. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What three things does the access check compare? + The process's token, the object's security descriptor, and the rights requested - The user's password, the file's name and the time of day - The process id, the thread id and the handle value - The program's signature, its version and its install folder > The token says who the process is, the descriptor says who may do what, and the request says what is wanted now. ? What is the principle of least privilege? - Running every program as administrator so nothing fails + Requesting and holding only the rights the code actually needs - Giving the most important process the highest priority - Letting only one user log on at a time > Asking for less means requests succeed for ordinary users, and a compromised program can do less harm. ? What is a protected process? - A process that cannot crash - A process running with administrator rights - A process whose window cannot be closed + One the kernel shields even from administrators > Anti-cheat and DRM components often run this way. The protection comes from the kernel, not from rights on the object. Its memory cannot be read, injected into or debugged by other processes. ? When does Windows check whether you may write to a file? - On every single write call, by looking at the user's groups again - Never: files are not secured + When the handle is opened with write access requested > The access check happens at open time. ? A program running as a normal user asks for `GENERIC_ALL` on a file it may only read. What happens? + The open fails with access denied - It gets a handle with read access only - It gets full access anyway > Windows grants all of the requested rights or none. ? What does UAC elevation change? - It makes the program run faster + The process gets the full administrator token - It turns off the access check > Without elevation, an administrator's programs run with the administrator group disabled. ? Why can even an administrator not read the memory of a protected process? - Its security descriptor is empty - Protected processes have no memory + The kernel enforces it whatever the caller's token > Protected Process Light shields security components from tampering. ```
ideas:
- Try to open `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` with `GENERIC_WRITE` as a normal user and describe the error. Then open it with `GENERIC_READ`.
- Use `OpenProcess` with `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` on a few process ids from lesson 6.07's list, then with `PROCESS_VM_READ`, and compare which succeed.
- Open Process Explorer from Sysinternals and look at your program's Security tab: its integrity level and the groups in its token.

cards.q: What three things does the access check compare?
cards.a:
The process's token, the object's security descriptor, and the rights requested

The token says who the process is, the descriptor says who may do what, and the request says what is wanted now.

cards.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
cards.a:
Requesting and holding only the rights the code actually needs

Asking for less means requests succeed for ordinary users, and a compromised program can do less harm.

One the kernel shields even from administrators

Anti-cheat and DRM components often run this way. The protection comes from the kernel, not from rights on the object. Its memory cannot be read, injected into or debugged by other processes.

cards.q: When does Windows check whether you may write to a file?
cards.a:
When the handle is opened with write access requested

The access check happens at open time.

cards.q: A program running as a normal user asks for `GENERIC_ALL` on a file it may only read. What happens?
cards.a:
The open fails with access denied

Windows grants all of the requested rights or none.

The process gets the full administrator token

Without elevation, an administrator's programs run with the administrator group disabled.

cards.q: Why can even an administrator not read the memory of a protected process?
cards.a:
The kernel enforces it whatever the caller's token

Protected Process Light shields security components from tampering.
